description.narrative:
The contribution aims to advance human rights in Kosovo by addressing critical issues in labor rights, mental health, using strategic litigation as a key tool. Built on a deep understanding of the human rights landscape, the project employs evidence-based strategies and fosters collaborative partnerships to uphold the principles of justice, equality, and dignity for all.
The contribution will be implemented in partnership with carefully chosen implementing civil society organizations that have a proven track record of success in achieving project goals. In addition, other governmental institutions will have a key role in the implementation such as as the Labour Inspectorate, Ministry of Health, and the Ombudsperson, as well as other committed stakeholders from which to mention the International Laobur Organisation, ILO. Each of these partners brings invaluable expertise and experience, which are essential for advancing human rights and driving meaningful social change in Kosovo. Furthermore by fostering a culture of trust and cooperation, these partners ensure that joint planning and co-design processes are effective. This synergy allows all parties to work toward shared goals with a unified vision and strong commitment, maximizing the intervention's impact and helping to realize the principles of justice, equality, and dignity for all.
Labour Right Objective - To promote labour practices and create a more inclusive work environment in Kosovo by actively involving the public and business sectors through the enforcement of labour laws and regulations, promotion of union representation, combating workplace discrimination, fostering dialogue and consultation and raising awareness.
Mental Health Objective - To enhance open discussions around mental health in Kosovo and cultivate a culture of acceptance while improving the accessibility, effectiveness and support for services that uphold the dignity of individuals facing mental health challenges.
Strategic Litigation Objective - To enhance the protection and promotion of human rights in Kosovo through sustained strategic litigation services.
The project objectives: Labour rights - Mental Health and Strategic Litigation are designed to work together, leveraging strengths to promote human rights.

Genom Human Rightivism-projektet ger CDF civilsamhällesorganisationer resurser för att utmana konservativa normer och förespråka progressiv förändring. Framöver kommer CDF att fokusera på psykisk hälsa, arbetstagares rättigheter och strategiska rättstvister, med målet att förbättra arbetsvillkor, främja rättvisa arbetsförhållanden och öka stödet för individer som lider av psykisk ohälsa. Denna insats ligger i linje med Sveriges regionala reformstrategi och syftar till att främja ett rättvist och jämlikt samhälle i Kosovo. Genom att stärka arbetsrättsligt skydd, stödja mentalvårdstjänster och använda strategiska rättstvister bidrar CDF till meningsfull systemisk förändring och främjandet av mänskliga rättigheter. Det evidensbaserade tillvägagångssättet och synergierna mellan institutioner och civilsamhällesorganisationer pekar ytterligare på vikten av denna insats, vilken inte bara syftar till att uppnå omedelbara resultat utan också till att främja långvarig verkan, hållbarhet och förtroendeskapande.

Through the Human Rightivism project, CDF empowers CSOs with resources to challenge conservative norms and advocate for progressive change. Moving forward, CDF will focus on mental health, labour rights and strategic litigation, aiming to enhance working conditions, promote fair labor practices, and expand mental health support. This initiative, aligns with Sweden’s regional reform strategy and aims to foster a just and equitable society in Kosovo. By strengthening labor protections, supporting mental health services, and employing strategic litigation, CDF contributes to meaningful systemic change and the advancement of human rights. Furthermore, the evidence-based approach and synergy between institutional and CSO sectors highlight the importance of this initiative, not only for achieving immediate results but also for fostering lasting impact, sustainability, and trust-building.

The Human Rightivism Project implemented by the Community Development Fund (CDF) concluded a strong and measurable set of achievements across all thematic areas, combining service delivery, capacity building, policy influence, and community engagement, with both expected and unexpected results clearly demonstrated. In terms of expected results, the project concluded substantial progress across sectors:
In labor rights, 21 awareness activities engaged 431 participants (179 women and 252 men), with 82.5% reporting improved understanding of labor rights issues. In addition, 146 workers were reached through workplace-based dialogue sessions. Institutional strengthening was concluded through 6 training sessions for 20 labor inspectors, where 100% reported improved knowledge, and 94.4% reported increased capacity to identify discrimination. Field monitoring concluded 30 labor inspections, producing evidence on systemic gaps, while over 15 advocacy outputs ensured continued public visibility. In mental health, the project concluded 1,214 crisis calls and 166 referrals through the Lifeline platform. Capacity building reached 192 first responders, with 89.7% reporting improved knowledge and confidence, while 25 journalists and editors were trained, with 95% reporting improved ethical awareness. Community interventions concluded with an anxiety support group of 26 participants, where 100% reported improved wellbeing and reduced isolation. Furthermore, 18 documented human rights cases and a major national report were completed, strengthening evidence-based advocacy. In strategic litigation, the project concluded high-impact legal results, including Supreme Court decisions affecting administrative practices and protecting approximately 35,000 citizens annually. CSL concluded management of 1315 strategic cases, submitted 20 policy recommendations, and delivered lectures to 36 students, where 100% reported improved understanding of human rights mechanisms.
In social inclusion, women represented 41.5% of participants in labor rights activities, while targeted support concluded assistance to 6 survivors of gender-based violence, 5 youth beneficiaries, and 33 elderly participants, with all groups reporting 100% improvements in wellbeing, skills, or coping capacity. A major conclusion was also the expansion of the small grants scheme, which received over 130 applications and concluded with 32 awarded grants, significantly exceeding initial expectations and enabling nationwide grassroots action.
In conclusion, several unexpected results were also observed. Youth engagement in vocational centres worked better than expected, showing strong participation and offering a useful way to support labour rights education. Community-based mental health activities also led to positive results, with most participants reporting satisfaction and improved wellbeing. The small grants expansion was also an unexpected success, showing strong demand and active involvement from civil society. Overall, the project delivered not only measurable results but also clear improvements in awareness, institutional capacity, and civic engagement.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
